title: The myth of best practice: how understanding the site changes what best fits
text_snippet: The myth of best practice: how understanding the site changes what best fits Abstract This article problematises the discourses of ‘best practice’, and despite the prevalence of the term in educational media and policy, there is a general lack of consensus how it is reconciled by teachers as they seek to understand and develop their pedagogical practices. By applying practice theory as a site-ontological lens through which to understand education practices, analysis of observations of teacher professional learning conversations and follow-up interviews and focus groups, an empirical basis to reframe best practice as best-fit practice is proposed. Findings from one case selected from a two-year ethnographic case study conducted in seven schools show how a site ontological perspective reframes best practice not as a universal set of rules, procedures or programs but as best-fit practices , those that are uniquely relevant to particular places, at particular times and with particular groups of learners (both teachers and students). This reframing asserts a principled, dynamic, site-based and responsive approach to practice, ever open to focused professional critique and reflection. title: Leading Australian early childhood education and care through crises and complexity
text_snippet: Leading Australian early childhood education and care through crises and complexity Abstract This qualitative study investigated how leadership in early childhood education and care (ECEC) is enacted during times of crisis and complexity including the COVID-19 pandemic, climate disasters, and community tragedies. Sixteen Australian ECEC leaders participated in the study that comprised twelve Dialogic Café sessions over six months. The participant-driven inquiry foregrounded their experience of leading through crises. Using complexity leadership theory as an analytical lens, the study revealed adaptive, enabling, and administrative leadership practices that foster resilience, innovation, and community care. An important finding was the identification of the depth of the emotional labour performed by leaders, often invisible, yet critical to sustaining services and community wellbeing. The study findings signal the need for leadership preparation that reflects the realities of complexity, and for systemic support including policy co-design and emotional wellbeing initiatives. Although this study has an Australian context, findings and implications hold relevance internationally where escalating climate and political crises imply growing complexity for ECEC leaders.

title: Authorial voice in human–machine writing with GenAI: plays and counterplays of meaning
text_snippet: Authorial voice in human–machine writing with GenAI: plays and counterplays of meaning Abstract Writing is a means of negotiating and expressing human identity and authorial voice. With the increased availability of GenAI technologies to automate writing processes, a critical examination of the transformed relations between identity and authorial voice is urgently needed. In this paper, we apply a critical walkthrough methodology with the paid, advanced application—ChatGPT 4.5—to explore how authorial voice can be shaped through human-AI interaction. By applying a reflexive model of GenAI-integrated writing, we examine AI-generated texts and the potential alignments or gaps in the resulting written text with respect to authorial intentions. The analysis discusses prompts used to compose writing aligned with authorial voice, to demonstrate how human authors assert their presence, express their values, and align or distance themselves from particular positions available in generated texts. The paper outlines implications for the pedagogical adaptation of GenAI for writing, emphasing the use of GenAI applications for writing that strengthen authorial voice by generating texts that prioritise human agency and consider polyvocal perspectives.

title: A missing player: the absence of Indigenous video games in schools
text_snippet: A missing player: the absence of Indigenous video games in schools Abstract Whilst the use of video games in education is not an innovative field of study, the use of Indigenous video games is. Understanding how, and if, Indigenous developed video games are used in classrooms can aid in the identification of support for teachers and the benefits for students, particularly regarding colonial and decolonial discourse. Research in this space is limited, highlighting a significant gap in the literature. A two-stage scoping review of research regarding the application of Indigenous video games in schools was undertaken which also identified communities leading the way in this space. The analysis of captured literature identified North America, Aotearoa (New Zealand) and Australia yielded the most results in the use of Indigenous video games in education. A common theme amongst the research demonstrated the prevalence of settler colonial narratives within video games, and how Indigenous-made video games were pushing back against this rhetoric. These findings highlight the need for Indigenous-made video games to be used more widely within education to prompt critical thinking in students, especially in reference to colonial discourse in digital spaces. title: ‘We’re cannibalising each other’: a case study of teacher turnover in hard-to-staff schools
text_snippet: ‘We’re cannibalising each other’: a case study of teacher turnover in hard-to-staff schools Abstract In this paper, we present a case study of hard-to-staff secondary schools to examine teacher turnover in Australia. The paper draws on interviews with teachers and school leaders to explore issues related to turnover, an aspect of workforce instability that is less recognised in discussions of the Australian teaching workforce. We situate this analysis within the broader context of education marketisation to consider the implications for disadvantaged schools in the context of widespread teacher shortages. We map the dynamics of localised experiences of turnover, highlighting the impacts of marketisation on the teaching workforce through increasing competition between schools for teachers, the ongoing process of continuous recruitment, and the complexities of teacher retention in hard-to-staff schools. We demonstrate how this cycle of constant staff replacement not only disrupts school stability and social relationships but also places additional strain on remaining teachers and leaders, creating unsustainable working environments that further drive turnover contributing to increasingly stratified working conditions for teachers across different school contexts.

title: A systematic integrative review methodology using phenomenographic analysis: bridging empirical and theoretical literature in educational research, with an exemplar protocol on educational purpose
text_snippet: A systematic integrative review methodology using phenomenographic analysis: bridging empirical and theoretical literature in educational research, with an exemplar protocol on educational purpose Abstract Educational researchers and policymakers require robust literature review and analysis methodologies capable of engaging with complexity. This paper presents a novel systematic integrative review methodology in tandem with phenomenographic analysis methods to explore diverse concepts, and wicked problems. Traditional approaches to literature reviews may fail to integrate diverse literature types, especially when addressing complex educational phenomena. In addition, the ‘difficult to define’ aspect of complex concepts that often lie at the heart of wicked problems require appropriate analytic methods. This methodological duo is illustrated in a protocol examining recent literature on the purposes of school-based education (2000–2025). The protocol may support first principles exploration of other wicked problems by mapping diverse bodies of literature and conceptions. The methodology integrates diverse types of literature and uniquely treats research papers as primary data for phenomenographic analysis. It adopts a five-stage framework: problem identification, literature search, data evaluation, analysis, and presentation, and utilises phenomenography as its analytical len

title: STEM in the early years: rethinking teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge
text_snippet: STEM in the early years: rethinking teachers’ pedagogical content knowledge Abstract Neoliberal reforms increasingly frame early childhood education and care (ECEC) as an investment in human capital, with science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) education prioritised from the earliest years of learning. This policy orientation draws attention to teachers’ content knowledge, as scientific concepts require explicit guidance beyond experiential exploration. Traditionally, however, ECEC has emphasised holistic development and learning, deliberately eschewing narrow, subject-based approaches. Within this context, research has raised questions about teachers’ subject knowledge and confidence in teaching STEM. Such concerns tend to reflect conventional definitions of professional knowledge and are reinforced by gendered assumptions about STEM expertise. Focusing on computational thinking (CT) as pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), this study reports on a pilot STEM professional learning program informed by survey data and focus group discussions. It argues for a dynamic understanding of PCK in ECEC, recognising teachers’ expertise as relational, context-dependent and continually evolving.

title: Rethinking teacher professionalism through the capability approach: responding to superdiversity in education
text_snippet: Rethinking teacher professionalism through the capability approach: responding to superdiversity in education Abstract Recognition of increasing student diversity highlights the limitations of standards-based models of teacher professionalism. These frameworks often struggle to accommodate complexity, and risk reducing ethical and relational work to technical compliance and measurable outputs, thereby overlooking crucial qualities like care, autonomy, and situated judgement. This paper proposes the capability approach, initially developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, as a human-centred and justice-sensitive alternative for redefining teacher professionalism in superdiverse contexts. The capability approach shifts the evaluative focus from prescribed standards and outcomes to the real freedoms and opportunities (capabilities) teachers possess to be and do what they value as professionals. We argue for the normative and practical appeal of a capability-oriented model that would involve: (1) identifying valued professional functionings through participatory processes; (2) evaluating teachers’ real capabilities; and (3) understanding the personal, social, and environmental conversion factors affecting whether resources translate into substantive freedoms. title: The Nguluway of Knowledges Framework: weaving together Indigenous Institutional Theory and the 8 Aboriginal Ways of Learning
text_snippet: The Nguluway of Knowledges Framework: weaving together Indigenous Institutional Theory and the 8 Aboriginal Ways of Learning Abstract There is a push for Australian educational institutions to meaningfully weave together Indigenous and Western pedagogical approaches. Ideally, this synergy of pedagogical approaches would be reflected in curricula that authentically integrates Indigenous ways of learning and Community-informed content. Despite this educational push, few frameworks exist to guide meaningful integration of Indigenous pedagogy in Western institutions. Similarly, there is a need for Indigenous-designed theoretical underpinnings that are tailored to the interface between university education and institutional research contexts. The authors address gaps in educational theory by presenting an innovative conceptual framework, the Nguluway of Knowledges Framework. Nguluway, a Wiradjuri word meaning “meeting each other”, positions authentic Indigenous pedagogical approaches within Western educational structures. The conceptual framework weaves Indigenous ways of learning in Westernised institutions, such as universities, by bringing together Indigenous Institutional Theory (Coates et al., 2022) and the 8 Aboriginal Ways of Learning Framework (Yunkaporta, 2009). title: An exploration of VET in Schools programs and contributions to the STEM careers pipeline
text_snippet: An exploration of VET in Schools programs and contributions to the STEM careers pipeline Abstract STEM-based employment is projected to grow at almost twice the rate of other occupations; yet, there are persistent difficulties in meeting the demands for a STEM-skilled workforce. Further, there are well-established issues in STEM education that impact the pursuit of STEM careers by equity groups including girls, low-SES and non-metropolitan students. Attrition among these groups has been described as the “leaky pipeline”, characterised by students from such equity groups withdrawing from educational pathways that lead to STEM careers. A potential contributor to the STEM careers pipeline is STEM-aligned Vocational Education and Training (VET) programs delivered within secondary schools. The current study explores publicly available VET in Schools data to determine the participation of school-age students, including among equity groups (i.e. girls, low SES, and non-metropolitan students), in STEM-aligned programs. Overall, less than 5% of VET in Schools program completions were aligned to STEM careers; however, the completion of STEM-aligned programs has more than doubled in the last five years. title: “It has been an adventure and something I’ll remember forever”: insights from two Australian primary teachers participating in a 10-week Bush School program
text_snippet: “It has been an adventure and something I’ll remember forever”: insights from two Australian primary teachers participating in a 10-week Bush School program Abstract This study originated as an investigation into the impact of a 10-week nature play intervention on Year One students’ wellbeing, school engagement, sense of belonging, and academic performance. While positive student outcomes were anticipated, the findings also revealed unexpected effects on the two participating teachers. Using a qualitative case study approach, teachers’ lived experiences were explored through interviews, teacher journals, and researcher observations. Data were interpreted using reflexive thematic analysis to capture contextually grounded insights. Findings revealed strengthened teacher-student relationships, reduced behavioural management challenges, and a shift in teachers’ understanding of engagement. Teachers also reported emotional renewal and professional reflection; outcomes conceptually linked to teacher wellbeing, job satisfaction and retention. As a small case study at a single site, these findings provide preliminary insights into the professional experiences of teachers implementing nature play and suggest that such approaches may have important implications for teacher wellbeing, job satisfaction, and professional engagement.

title: Australian teachers and school leaders: improving learning outcomes for adolescent attention deficit hyperactivity disorder boys
text_snippet: Australian teachers and school leaders: improving learning outcomes for adolescent attention deficit hyperactivity disorder boys Abstract Many adolescent attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) boys find schooling unenjoyable and challenging. This small-scale, qualitative Australian study using individual semi-structured interviews reports on how teachers and school leaders in one alternative secondary school academically support the learning for adolescent ADHD boys in their classrooms. The analysis of data revealed one major theme of teaching and teacher strategies for optimum learning, along with four minor themes related to adjustments, technologies, ways to reduce distractions, and the optimum classroom environment. Findings showed that teachers and school leaders used a variety of innovative teaching practices and strategies to support the learning and academic needs of adolescent ADHD boys. The results provide starting points for more in-depth investigations into the kinds of alternative secondary schools that are a good fit for adolescent ADHD boys. title: Supporting Early Career Teachers: What’s the problem represented to be in England and South Australia?
text_snippet: Supporting Early Career Teachers: What’s the problem represented to be in England and South Australia? Abstract The widespread acceptance of the importance of supporting Early Career Teachers (ECTs) through mentoring, induction, and coaching is reflected in the proliferation of support programs for ECTs across many educational contexts. However, the policies that govern these programs in England and South Australia prioritise utilitarian outcomes such as workforce retention, rather than relying on the evidence base for supporting ECTs in a strengths-based and purpose-driven way. Bacchi's (2009) ‘What’s the problem represented to be?’ (WPR) framework was applied to 19 policy documents across England and South Australia relating to supporting ECTs from 2008 to 2025. The comparative approach and novel adaptation of an hermeneutic approach enhanced the rigour of analysis. It was found that each system’s positioning of initial teacher education affects how ECT support is represented in policy and, therefore, how solutions are proposed. Notably, in both jurisdictions a deficit view of ECTs prevails among the revealed problem representations. title: “LANTITE on an oily rag”. University perspectives of implementing external hurdles in initial teacher education courses
text_snippet: “LANTITE on an oily rag”. University perspectives of implementing external hurdles in initial teacher education courses Abstract The aim of this study was to investigate how two universities designed and implemented student support structures for the Literacy and Numeracy Test Initial Teacher Education (LANTITE) a high-stakes licensure test. It identifies the challenges and opportunities they encountered when establishing processes to support the administrative and academic components, using a narrative approaches to elicit accounts of their experiences. Findings suggest each university faced unique challenges related to funding, staffing, communications, managing unsuccessful attempts, and data management. The universities identified opportunities, including the integration of professional learning within existing course delivery, securing external funding to support the development of LANTITE-specific resources, and accessing peer-support from other LANTITE coordinators located across Australia. title: The guidance officer as ‘middle ground’ : charting the positioning and positionalities of guidance officers in Queensland schools
text_snippet: The guidance officer as ‘middle ground’ : charting the positioning and positionalities of guidance officers in Queensland schools Abstract Working at the intersection of student counselling, case management, school-wide wellbeing coordination and support programming, guidance officers assume a specialised presence in schools, maintaining responsibility for some of the most complex and challenging of circumstances in student support. Yet, and despite the responsibilities and quantum of work that guidance officers bear, it occurs that guidance officers typically work individually or in small, specialised teams. Occupying this ‘middle ground’ of specialised practice and close engagement with students generates specific pressures that demonstrate the complexities inherent to guidance work. This paper reports on the viewpoints of a cohort of guidance officers ( n = 13) currently employed in Queensland schools to detail the nature of the roles they fulfil. The paper observes that the guidance officer role could be more meaningfully recognised in contemporary school settings and that potential exists for recognising the specialisation of their practice and the interstitial locations they occupy.

title: Understanding contemporary digital childhoods in Australia: A bounded scoping review of transdisciplinary research of the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child
text_snippet: Understanding contemporary digital childhoods in Australia: A bounded scoping review of transdisciplinary research of the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child Abstract Childhoods are shaped by people, experiences, and contexts that, increasingly, include if and how children connect with digital technology. This scoping review, bounded by the research of a national Centre of Excellence that is currently the largest critical mass of transdisciplinary research about Australian digital childhoods, asked: What insights and understandings about contemporary digital childhoods in Australia can be drawn from the research of the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child? Sixty-one studies (15 reviews and 46 primary studies) met the inclusion criteria of being a peer-reviewed publication of primary research or a structured review associated with the Centre. Results were synthesised in three clusters, derived from the trial of various inductive and deductive classification schemes, as (1) children ( k = 16), (2) children’s adults ( k = 30), and (3) surrounding systems that shape digital childhoods ( k = 15). Within-cluster inductive narrative synthesis enabled thematic analysis that accounted for the breadth of design, discipline, focus, and methodologies within the archive. title: Safe harbours in treacherous waters: Leading pride groups in schools
text_snippet: Safe harbours in treacherous waters: Leading pride groups in schools Abstract Pride groups are widely recognised in international literature as fostering inclusion, improving school climate, and reducing bias-based bullying for LGBTIQA + youth. This qualitative study explores how leadership of school-based pride groups in Tasmanian public schools is understood and practised by key stakeholders. Drawing on the thematic analysis of interviews with school staff and focus groups with pride group participants, the research highlights the transformative potential of these student-led groups. Our findings affirm this outcome in the Tasmanian context, with students describing pride groups as essential spaces of safety, belonging, and affirmation in school environments that often remain hostile or unsupportive. At the same time, the findings highlight the structural limitations that constrain these groups. Pride groups are frequently hampered by reliance on voluntary staff labour, inconsistent institutional recognition, and narrow policy framings that valourise visible, student-led leadership while overlooking the relational and emotional labour young people perform. title: An examination of behaviour support advice on Australian state and territory government education department websites
text_snippet: An examination of behaviour support advice on Australian state and territory government education department websites Abstract Disruptive or challenging student behaviour in Australian schools continues to attract attention. Recent reports have raised concerns about a rise in behaviour incidents involving aggression and disruption. At the same time, many teachers report feeling ill-equipped to deal with common behavioural challenges, despite the existence of proven strategies to support and respond to student behaviour. While moves are underway to include evidence-based classroom management content in pre-service teacher training courses, responsibility for upskilling existing teachers rests predominantly with education systems. One way that education systems communicate policy direction and influence teacher practice is through the provision of information and guidance on corporate websites. We therefore conducted a search of the websites of state and territory education departments for the presence of information and advice aligning with an evidence-based approach to student behaviour. title: Multiculturalism, the cultural interface and migrant teachers
text_snippet: Multiculturalism, the cultural interface and migrant teachers Abstract Multicultural diversity in settler-colonial Australia impacts the way that the growing number of migrant teachers in Australia’s teaching workforce engage in Indigenous education. Foundational ideas of multiculturalism promote diversity and inclusion yet can inadvertently perpetuate the narratives of settler colonialism. The impact is that the important decolonial work required to prevent Indigenous erasure is further impeded. Drawing on Nakata’s (2007) concept of the cultural interface, this paper illustrates how migrant teachers navigate complex knowledge-power dynamics shaped by Indigenous sovereignty, white colonial privilege, and multicultural diversity. Literature from these fields illustrates the knowledge contestations required for migrant teachers to engage effectively in Indigenous education. Multicultural diversity, when uncritically aligned with white colonial privilege, can reinforce systemic barriers to Indigenous representation and sovereignty in education. title: Learning, play, and the shifting expectations of childhood: insights from young children in Australian schools
text_snippet: Learning, play, and the shifting expectations of childhood: insights from young children in Australian schools Abstract The experience of childhood is not static. It is subject to changing social, cultural, and economic demands. In 2009, the Australian Government heeded the advice of internationally acclaimed economists and ‘reconceptualised’ childhood as a critical period for investment to secure a stronger economic future. In response, a revised school-based childhood emerged, echoing neoliberal ideology through a national curriculum that heightened focus on the “well-being” and “well-becoming” of young children. Alteration to the expectations of school-based childhood in Australia beckons researchers to examine the undiluted perspectives of young children. Using a qualitative approach, visual-dialogic methodology supported by children’s drawn and embodied expressions were used to capture and understand the views of 17 public school children aged 5 and 6 years old in Western Australia. The children explained their experience of childhood and then their understanding of how children learn. They celebrated play as what children do . title: Commercial curriculum, efficiency claims and teachers’ work: a systematic research synthesis
text_snippet: Commercial curriculum, efficiency claims and teachers’ work: a systematic research synthesis Abstract This paper presents a systematic literature synthesis examining commercial curriculum resources and their effects on teachers’ workload, with a specific focus on lesson planning and preparation time. The review develops a typology spanning commercially published curriculum materials, including textbooks, scripted programs, online repositories, digital platforms, and more recently GenAI tools. Across resource types, the dominant policy and provider claim is that externally produced materials deliver a time dividend by reducing planning and preparation time. Our synthesis finds that evidence of sustained workload relief is limited and highly conditional. While some resources reduce ‘from scratch’ preparation, time is commonly shifted into hidden labour such as searching, quality-checking, curriculum alignment, contextualisation and accountability compliance. These dynamics also reshape teacher professionalism: highly prescriptive resources can narrow autonomy, while discretionary use can support adaptive curriculum-making. title: Using activity theory to identify contradictions impacting mentoring in schools following mentor training
text_snippet: Using activity theory to identify contradictions impacting mentoring in schools following mentor training Abstract This research adopted an activity theory lens to analyse the implementation of a teacher mentor training program. The aim of the research was to understand how contradictions within the mentoring activity system impacted on the implementation of mentoring in school contexts. The Teacher Mentor Training (TMT) program (pseudonym) was developed as a systemic response to national and state government reviews of teacher education in Australia. The TMT program ran for six years in one Australian state with over 4000 teachers participating in the two-day face-to-face program. On completion of the program, teachers were expected to act as leads in mentoring back in their schooling contexts. As the mentor training program was a system-wide initiative with substantial government investment of fiscal and human resources, equitable implementation of mentoring in schools across the sector was expected, along with sustained impacts of the program. Data were collected three years after the program ceased via interviews with teacher mentors who completed the TMT program. title: Enhancing civic engagement and Indigenous knowledge integration in Australian universities: a framework for strengthening ‘Closing the Gap’ and addressing national Indigenous research priorities
text_snippet: Enhancing civic engagement and Indigenous knowledge integration in Australian universities: a framework for strengthening ‘Closing the Gap’ and addressing national Indigenous research priorities Abstract Australian universities operate within a national context defined by ongoing disparities in Indigenous outcomes, as outlined by the ‘Closing the Gap’ framework. This paper argues that a fundamental change is necessary in how these institutions conceptualise and practice civic engagement, as well as moving towards incorporating Indigenous knowledges. By analysing existing Indigenous Strategy and Indigenous Research Strategies across Australian universities alongside an Indigenous rights-based approach (IRBA), this paper presents a comprehensive framework for universities to move beyond superficial reconciliation towards genuine decolonial transformation. Embedding Indigenous intellectual agency, establishing community-led governance, and adopting ethical, rights-based methodologies, including culturally responsive artificial intelligence (AI), can help universities better contribute to ‘Closing the Gap’ targets, align with national Indigenous research priorities, and authentically meet the research needs of Indigenous peoples and communities. title: Carrying the weight of caring: exploring compassion fatigue among teachers in trauma-affected classrooms
text_snippet: Carrying the weight of caring: exploring compassion fatigue among teachers in trauma-affected classrooms Abstract Compassion fatigue, a psychological burden arising from sustained empathetic engagement, significantly impacts teachers, particularly those working with trauma-affected students. This study investigates how Australian teachers experience and navigate compassion fatigue through the lens of compassion fatigue theory and Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory. Using qualitative data from 57 educators via an online questionnaire, the study explores the interplay of emotional, cognitive, and systemic factors influencing compassion fatigue. Thematic analysis revealed four key themes: emotional and cognitive challenges, systemic and institutional demands, personal resilience and professional satisfaction, and balancing personal and professional life. Findings underscore that compassion fatigue extends beyond individual emotional struggles to include systemic pressures, such as excessive workloads, inadequate institutional support, and the undervaluation of teachers’ emotional labour. title: Zoo visits as catalysts for science identity: informal learning and career aspirations among grade 3–7 students in South Africa
text_snippet: Zoo visits as catalysts for science identity: informal learning and career aspirations among grade 3–7 students in South Africa Abstract Informal learning experiences can spark dreams that classroom lessons alone may not ignite. This qualitative study investigated how a zoo visit influenced the science-related career aspirations of Grade 3–7 students in South Africa. Guided by social cognitive career theory and possible selves theory, the study explored students’ experiences of engagement, meaning-making, and emerging aspirations through interviews, drawings, and classroom observations with 25 students and five teachers from five schools. Findings revealed that the zoo visit stimulated high levels of enthusiasm, enriched scientific understanding, and inspired students to imagine futures as scientists, veterinarians, and conservationists. Positive emotional experiences and mastery-oriented learning strengthened students’ self-efficacy and expanded their possible selves in science education. However, teachers seldom linked the experience formally to curriculum goals, highlighting missed opportunities for deeper integration. title: Transformative change or status quo? An investigation of the Senate Inquiry recommendations on policy and practice regarding school refusal in Australia
text_snippet: Transformative change or status quo? An investigation of the Senate Inquiry recommendations on policy and practice regarding school refusal in Australia Abstract One of the most significant challenges currently facing education in Australia, and globally, is the decline in school attendance rates, along with a growing awareness of the associated harm being done to many children in attending school environments. Much policy attention is now focused on declining attendance, including a recent Australian Government Senate Inquiry into school refusal. Using a transformational change through public policy framework, this paper analyses the recommendations of this Senate Inquiry to understand their potential to deliver transformational change. We find some potential for a systemic, cross-sectoral approach that builds change through many incremental actions. However, there is little scope for reconceptualising the problem and generating novel solutions. The recommendations present a pattern of imposing a single top-down framework with limited room for diverse perspectives, and do not incorporate the knowledge of those with lived experience, including parents and carers. Overall, the Inquiry’s outcomes appear more likely to reinforce the status quo than drive transformative change.

title: Regional homeschool children’s experience with arts-based digital literacy workshops
text_snippet: Regional homeschool children’s experience with arts-based digital literacy workshops Abstract The number of children engaged in homeschool education is increasing, particularly in regional areas of Australia. Homeschool families currently access community-based activities such as theatre productions and sports programs, as well as public library services, to enrich their children’s learning. However, access to quality programs that support digital literacy skills remains limited and the benefits of these programs to home schoolers remain largely unexplored. This study examined the experiences of homeschool families with children aged 6–12 who participated in a series of stop-motion animation workshops held in a regional Western Australian public library. Data were collected from both participating parents and children via reflection sheets, semi-structured interviews and researcher observations. Findings indicated that the workshops enhanced children’s digital literacy and empowered their parents with new skills and pedagogies to integrate into their homeschooling practices. title: The possibilities and pitfalls of curricular autonomy and curricular prescription: seeking a balance point
text_snippet: The possibilities and pitfalls of curricular autonomy and curricular prescription: seeking a balance point Abstract An important debate in curriculum research is that over the merits of more prescriptive versus more flexible curricula. This paper draws on two case studies–one from Aotearoa New Zealand’s high-autonomy curricular environment and the other from a more centralised environment in New South Wales, Australia–to advance understanding of the affordances and limitations of these two types of contexts for teacher practice. Biesta’s (2021) notion of ‘world-centred education’ is used as an ideal against which to assess teacher curriculum making within each curricular ecosystem. Findings suggest that both flexibility and prescription have distinct benefits and limitations. Flexibility may foster attention to students’ unique contexts, but risk de-emphasising important knowledge, sufficient challenge and breadth of content, while prescription can support consistency but lead to ‘curriculum overload’ and constrain deeper engagement with material. Rather than advocating for one model over another, this paper calls for a nuanced approach to curriculum that recognises the need for a ‘balance point’ between flexibility and standardisation. title: Place-taking or space-making: immigrant parents’ and career advisers’ perspectives on youth workplace learning in Aotearoa New Zealand
text_snippet: Place-taking or space-making: immigrant parents’ and career advisers’ perspectives on youth workplace learning in Aotearoa New Zealand Abstract In this research, we draw on Das Gupta’s theory of immigrants’ negotiation of transnational rights and borders. Specifically, we follow the two key notions of her work, place-taking and space-making , to explore secondary school immigrant students’ engagement with work experience as part of their school curriculum and their transition from school to work or tertiary education. While work experience is widely recognised as critical for school-to-work transitions, immigrant youth often face systemic barriers. This research asks: How do parents and career advisers act as place-takers or space-makers in enabling or constraining these opportunities? We explore whether parents and career advisers function as place-takers (reinforcing barriers) or space-makers (creating opportunities), and how their roles intersect with systemic inequities. Through semi-structured interviews with 16 immigrant parents and six career advisers, we find that parents often prioritise academic achievement over workplace learning, reinforcing place-taking norms, while economic pressures (e.g., pandemic-related instability) occasionally compel space-making adaptations. title: Visions and decisions: parents of children with disability visioning and navigating the education journey
text_snippet: Visions and decisions: parents of children with disability visioning and navigating the education journey Abstract From as early as a prenatal or postnatal diagnosis, parents of a child with Down syndrome begin considering potential educational futures. It is not as simple as pursuing what a child is legally entitled to or what the research evidence supports; there are a range of internal and external properties that influence parents’ hopes, goals, and decisions. This constructivist grounded theory research involved 32 parents (from 28 families) across four Australian states to analyse their main concerns and actions in relation to the education of their child with Down syndrome. The experiences of these parents, whose children were in the primary or secondary school years across a range of settings, can be theorised as a process of visioning and navigating the education journey, with three core categories of findings: Visioning a Preferred Path ; Navigating the Visioned Journey; and Re-visioning the Route. Findings provide insight into the complexities of planning and implementing schooling for a child with disability, which can inform reforms required within schools and education systems.

title: University missions and financial incentives: the response of universities to Australia’s Job-ready Graduates policy
text_snippet: University missions and financial incentives: the response of universities to Australia’s Job-ready Graduates policy Abstract Funding incentives are widely used to steer universities towards meeting policy objectives, but they do not always produce the expected outcomes. The headline policy of Australia’s Job-ready Graduates (JRG) university policy was the change to student fees, lower for priority ‘job ready’ disciplines and higher for others, to steer student course choices towards national priorities. JRG also significantly changed funding arrangements from a university perspective, in ways that sometimes contradicted the student incentives. How universities responded to JRG incentives and constraints remains unexplored. Drawing upon the critical lenses of policy enactment and policy instrumentation, this study examines university responses to the JRG policy. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with vice-chancellors and other senior staff at five universities to explore how institutional actors interpreted and negotiated the JRG policy within broader socio-political and institutional contexts. Three key findings are identified. First, earning a maximum university-level grant amount under JRG was widely (re)interpreted as a minimum, which contributed to enrolling additional students witho

title: “Keep that connection strong”: principal and staff perceptions on school belonging in regional schools
text_snippet: “Keep that connection strong”: principal and staff perceptions on school belonging in regional schools Abstract School belonging in regional, remote and rural (RRR) communities has been shown to be strong, despite geographic, social and structural factors that constrain access to resources and opportunities. This highlights the need to understand school belonging through a context-sensitive lens, which considers the entanglement of structural factors with the relational strengths of RRR communities. Drawing on focus groups and interviews with principals and staff across three regional schools in New South Wales, Australia, this study explored how school belonging is understood and what contextual factors are perceived as fostering or hindering it. Guided by Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory, thematic analysis revealed that school belonging emerges from the complex ecological interplay among school-level practices, interpersonal relationships, community context, and wider structural influences. Specifically, three key elements were emphasised as informing understandings of school belonging: helping students find a sense of purpose, pride and identification with school and the centrality of relationships. School belonging was perceived as fostered through supporting individua

title: Refugee-background students’ biographical perspectives as the enablers of praxis in Australia’s EAL/D classrooms: a scoping review
text_snippet: Refugee-background students’ biographical perspectives as the enablers of praxis in Australia’s EAL/D classrooms: a scoping review Abstract This scoping review explored refugee-background students’ biographical perspectives, including their lived histories, experiences, and linguistic, cultural, and social capital, as enabling praxis in Australia’s English as an Additional Language/Dialect EAL/D classrooms. Guided by Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, 25 studies (2010–2025) were systematically reviewed. Grounded in a praxis-oriented and intra-categorical understanding of diversity, this study conceptualises biographical perspectives (BPs) as relational constructs shaping how refugee-background students (RBS) think, act, and relate within the EAL/D classroom. Analysis revealed four interrelated themes: lived histories and forms of capital, resource mobilisation, visibility, and belonging, showing that BPs operate relationally across these dimensions. The reviewed studies conceptualised RBS’ BPs as individual resources for participation and learning. Yet they overlooked their structural and relational dimensions, leaving a conceptual gap between recognising BPs as habitus and theorising it as praxis shaped by power and inequality. Accordingly, these studies lacked the use of a praxis-orie

title: Teaching difficult Indigenous topics through textual analysis: a demonstration of metalogue in secondary English
text_snippet: Teaching difficult Indigenous topics through textual analysis: a demonstration of metalogue in secondary English Abstract In this paper, we replicate and reflect on the experience of using dialogue to engage with difficult Indigenous topics in a secondary English classroom. Although we are a group of three experienced teachers from diverse familial and professional backgrounds, we take on the role of secondary school English students enacting a metalogue on a difficult Indigenous topic. Specifically, we focus on the pamphlet circulated by the Australian Government to all households in 2023, which provided detailed information about the proposed constitutional changes to establish an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice. This pamphlet includes 4000 words of arguments from both the Yes and No camps, each presenting their case for or against the proposed law. Our research addressed two primary questions: (1) What emerges from the textual analysis of “The Pamphlet” when explored through a recursive dialogue? and (2) What practices enable respectful dialogue around the language features of “The Pamphlet” as a difficult knowledge text? Our textual analysis identified key textual features of “The Pamphlet”, including use of time as a persuasive device, repetition, and the interplay of logos,

title: From hermeneutic theory to pedagogical practice: dialogue, fusion of horizons, and tradition in the philosophy for children classroom
text_snippet: From hermeneutic theory to pedagogical practice: dialogue, fusion of horizons, and tradition in the philosophy for children classroom Abstract This article brings Hans-Georg Gadamer’s philosophical hermeneutics into critical conversation with the pedagogical practice of philosophy in schools, focusing particularly on Philosophy for Children (P4C). While P4C offers a rich pedagogical model for developing reasonableness through the Community of Inquiry (CoI), its account of the conditions under which understanding occurs remains somewhat underdeveloped. Although some scholars have situated P4C in relation to hermeneutics, this engagement is limited. Addressing this gap, the key Gadamerian ideas of tradition, prejudice, and the fusion of horizons and dialogue are explored here to deepen and extend the theoretical considerations of inquiry in P4C. The discussion argues that Gadamer’s theory of understanding as shaped by history and tradition challenges the ideal of facilitator neutrality associated with P4C. Gadamer’s reconceptualisation of prejudice as a productive condition of understanding reframes the teacher and student as historically constituted participants in open dialogue that raises questions and that leads to a ‘fusion of horizons’ where differing perspectives meet and reshape one another. title: Stakeholders’ views of the role of teacher assistants in inclusive education: insights from an online survey
text_snippet: Stakeholders’ views of the role of teacher assistants in inclusive education: insights from an online survey Abstract The inclusion of students with disabilities in regular schools has led to the widespread employment of teacher assistants to support learning, participation, and engagement. Despite their increasing presence, the role of teacher assistants remains poorly defined, with ongoing ambiguity surrounding their scope of practice and expectations. This lack of clarity contributes to inconsistent deployment, role confusion, and tensions within professional relationships. This study investigated how stakeholders perceive the role of teacher assistants in the context of inclusive education. The aim was to identify core responsibilities, clarify contested aspects, and highlight areas for improvement. A national online survey was conducted with a diverse cohort of respondents, including teacher assistants, teachers, school leaders, and other education professionals, from across Australian educational settings. The survey collected both quantitative and qualitative data, providing insight into areas of convergence and divergence regarding role responsibilities, training needs, and collaboration. The findings revealed persistent inconsistencies in how the role is defined, enacted, and sup

title: Examining the relationship between teacher career motivation and teacher job satisfaction: a multidimensional, multilevel approach
text_snippet: Examining the relationship between teacher career motivation and teacher job satisfaction: a multidimensional, multilevel approach Abstract Teachers choose to pursue a career in teaching for various reasons which might influence the extent to which they feel satisfied with their job. The relationship between teacher career motivation and teacher job satisfaction has been tested in some previous studies, but the findings have been inconsistent. In this study, we revisited this relationship by drawing on the Teaching and Learning International Survey 2018 data and adopting multilevel structural equation modelling as the main data analytic approach. Results suggest that the link between teacher career motivation and job satisfaction was more salient at the school level than at the teacher level. Schools in which teacher career choice was driven more by personal benefits reported lower school-average satisfaction whereas those where teachers showed stronger desire to support student learning and make social contributions had higher school-average satisfaction. The findings offer important implications for teacher recruitment and retention strategies and school improvement efforts.

title: Feeling heard and respected: relational trust and teacher wellbeing in Australian schools
text_snippet: Feeling heard and respected: relational trust and teacher wellbeing in Australian schools Abstract This qualitative study explores how Australian teachers experience relational trust in their everyday school relationships, how these experiences influence their wellbeing (if at all), and the factors that they describe as fostering or hindering trust. Guided by a social capital lens, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 11 teachers, and the data were thematically analysed. The findings show that when relational trust was strong, namely the confidence teachers have in their colleagues and leaders, teachers were more likely to feel safe, supported, valued, and secure in their roles. Trust was fostered in school environments that were calm, consistent, and predictable, with clear expectations, processes, values, and authentic collegial relationships. Conversely, teachers’ experiences of isolation, exclusion, inadequate support from school leaders, and limited opportunities for decision-making diminished trust, weakened social capital, and undermined wellbeing. Drawing on teachers’ voices, this study adds to the wellbeing literature by demonstrating how relational trust can serve as a foundation for promoting teacher wellbeing in the Australian context.

title: ‘I go in... I teach and I go home. I may as well be any other person. It would not make any difference’: experiences from the periphery of the academy
text_snippet: ‘I go in... I teach and I go home. I may as well be any other person. It would not make any difference’: experiences from the periphery of the academy Abstract Most academic staff in Australia are employed casually and on teaching-focused contracts, with little opportunity for research or advancement. This paper presents findings from a project undertaken at an Australian university and its pathway institution investigating casual academics’ experiences as peripheral members of the academy. Survey data from 59 casual academics and 13 follow-up interviews revealed several themes, including experiences of exclusion, lack of recognition and unpaid work. The study also found that most casual academics are women who experience intersectional marginalisation, being disadvantaged both as casual employees and as women, including due to ongoing caring responsibilities. Drawing on their lived experiences, the paper argues that casual academic staff often lack a sense of workplace belonging and inclusion. Yet they remain in precarious employment in the ‘hope’ of eventually securing a permanent academic position, even as identity characteristics such as gender restrict their capacity to engage in such labour and achieve these goals. The paper therefore offers recommendations for improving their working conditions and sense of belonging and p

title: An exploration of the cultural and structural influences on Year Coordinators’ vulnerability to compassion fatigue
text_snippet: An exploration of the cultural and structural influences on Year Coordinators’ vulnerability to compassion fatigue Abstract Young people in Australia are experiencing concerning levels of mental ill-health, with more than one in five reporting high psychological distress. As educators responsible for supporting students’ social and emotional wellbeing, Year Coordinators face frequent exposure to student distress alongside heavy teaching demands, placing them at heightened risk of compassion fatigue. Yet rather than acknowledging the structural forces that intensify this risk, compassion fatigue is often framed as an individual shortcoming. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 15 Year Coordinators across Australia to examine the systemic conditions shaping educators’ vulnerability to compassion fatigue. Using a Framework Method informed by critical neoliberal theory and scholarship on care work, findings reveal that the devaluation of care work and neoliberal logics in schooling leave educators managing complex workloads without adequate support. These insights have international significance as teachers globally are increasingly tasked with supporting students' mental health within similarly under-resourced systems.

title: Too hard, too confronting: the reluctance of schools to publicly acknowledge harm
text_snippet: Too hard, too confronting: the reluctance of schools to publicly acknowledge harm Abstract Despite having the largest caregiving responsibilities for children outside of families, schools are settings in which egregious forms of harm to children have occurred. As further allegations of non-recent and contemporary abuse of children in schools come to light, principals must decide whether to publicly acknowledge this harm and grapple with the complexities of how to do so. We examine what the research literature, recent public inquiries, and child safety policy reveal about the acknowledgement of harm in Victorian school settings, and identify a critical omission regarding how principals might manage such a response. We argue that public harm acknowledgement strengthens existing child protection cultures and practices and should be viewed by schools, child safety regulators, and governments as a way to foster a shared commitment to prevent past failures from recurring. To assist principals who choose to initiate public harm acknowledgement responses in the future, we call for urgent policy advice and guidance to help them navigate this challenging area of leadership.

title: The myth of instant readiness: temporal politics and subjectification in early-career teaching
text_snippet: The myth of instant readiness: temporal politics and subjectification in early-career teaching Abstract The myth of ‘instant readiness’, the assumption that graduate-teachers arrive as classroom-ready and fully formed, pervades contemporary teacher education policy. This article interrogates that myth through a narrative inquiry into one graduate-teacher’s first year in a socio-economically disadvantaged primary school. Tracing four critical-incidents across the year, the analysis examines how policy discourses of ‘classroom-readiness’, operationalised through the Teacher Performance Assessment, function as technologies of subjectification, imposing an ought self before the relational conditions for genuine professional becoming have been established. Drawing on Foucauldian analytics of power and Schutz et al.’s (2018) theorisation of ideal, actual, and ought selves, the findings expose ‘classroom-readiness’ as a temporal and political imposition that obscures the ethical and relational dimensions of early professional life. The article concludes by offering the concept of relational scaffolding as a necessary counterpoint to performative readiness frameworks, and as a foundation for rethinking sustainable early-career teaching.

title: Pre-service teachers’ wellbeing and occupational commitment: The role of motivation and coping
text_snippet: Pre-service teachers’ wellbeing and occupational commitment: The role of motivation and coping Abstract Given the growing concern regarding new teacher supply and the increasing demands for cultivating classroom-ready teachers, there is a pressing need to explore factors associated with pre-service teachers’ wellbeing. Yet exploration of the relationships between pre-service teachers’ motivation, self-beliefs, mental health, and job-related outcomes has been scarce. This study investigates the associations among motivational factors (autonomous motivation, controlled motivation, and self-efficacy), coping behaviours (engagement coping and disengagement coping), psychological wellbeing, and affective occupational commitment, which reflect the emotional attachment to the teaching profession. An integrative model of motivation and coping, synthesising self-determination theory and the cognitive-motivational-relational theory, was adapted for this analysis. In a sample of 677 pre-service teachers in Australia, structural equation modelling revealed that autonomous motivation and self-efficacy were positively associated with engagement coping and psychological wellbeing. Notably, autonomous motivation showed the strongest positive direct relationship with affective occupational c

title: ‘Someone you can run to’: teachers at the coalface of complex trauma
text_snippet: ‘Someone you can run to’: teachers at the coalface of complex trauma Abstract Recently, safeguarding children in early childhood has received widespread media coverage. This has shone a light on the critical work of early years teachers in supporting the learning, care and safety of young children. However, there has been limited exploration into what early years teachers actually do at the coalface to identify and support children with high levels of complex trauma. Drawing from a research project that examined early years teacher self-efficacy beliefs, this paper provides an analysis of the specific practices and beliefs of three early years teachers working in a complex, integrated early years site, in a disadvantaged community in Australia with a high number of children with complex trauma. Analysing segments of interview data collected over a 10-month period, findings revealed what the participants considered to be successful or challenging within their practice whilst working within a community shaped by complex trauma. This paper provides a hopeful account of the work of early years teachers and the role their teacher self-efficacy beliefs play in supporting children with complex trauma.

title: Making choices and having a go: facilitating young children’s creative agency with digital technologies
text_snippet: Making choices and having a go: facilitating young children’s creative agency with digital technologies Abstract Creativity is understood to be a vital attribute for success in an increasingly globalised and digitalised world. Educators play an important role in facilitating children’s creativity development through their considered choices of learning activities and pedagogy. For 21st century learners, the incorporation of digital technologies into the learning environment is also of rising importance. This study used observations of five children (4–8 years old) in Perth, Western Australia using digital technologies in their early learning environment. The ‘Person’ and ‘Process-Agency’ realms of Murcia et al.’s ‘A-E’ of Creativity framework were used to analyse whose creativity was being foregrounded in the activity, and the features of creative agency demonstrated by children when using the technologies. Findings suggest that when educators choose appropriate technologies and teach for creativity, children are able to demonstrate creative behaviours and their own creative thinking. However, when constrained by the affordances of the technology or the scope of the task, children’s creativity is limited. title: Identifying higher education research priorities at a regional Australian university: a modified-Delphi study
text_snippet: Identifying higher education research priorities at a regional Australian university: a modified-Delphi study Abstract Setting priorities is crucial for optimising research in resource-constrained environments, so we identify higher education (HE) research priorities at one regional Australian university. Employing constructivism, we conducted a three-round modified-Delphi with an expert panel (n = 64) using online questionnaires. Analysis included descriptive statistics (quantitative items), and content/theme analysis (qualitative). We collected 37 panellist-identified priorities (Round 1): the top three were AI in HE, how best to teach innovatively, and equity in HE. Across all three rounds, 48 priorities were considered with 31 achieving high importance and consensus: the top three were student engagement, how to teach creative/critical thinking skills, and how technology impacts HE. Key rationales underlying panellists’ priorities were conducting research to improve student learning, workforce preparedness, and aligning with institutional values. Findings align partly with international priority-setting exercises, but also reveal novel insights specific to the regional context. title: Making space for the unexpected: multimodal texts and serendipitous writing in early years and primary classrooms
text_snippet: Making space for the unexpected: multimodal texts and serendipitous writing in early years and primary classrooms Abstract Amid concerns about declining engagement in writing and a persistent focus on skills-based instruction, this study explores how multimodal texts can support both curriculum-aligned and serendipitous writing experiences in early years and primary classrooms. Drawing on a qualitative case study design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight early years and primary teachers across diverse geographical contexts in Queensland, Australia. Findings reveal that while multimodal texts were effective in supporting the teaching of writing knowledge and skills aligned with curriculum outcomes, the most powerful learning occurred when teachers created space for unexpected, child-initiated writing. These unexpected learning opportunities often led to rich, cross-curricular engagement and creative expression. In a policy climate shaped by standardised testing, this study underscores the importance of making pedagogical space for the unexpected, preserving opportunities for spontaneity, creativity, and child-led agency. title: Teachers’ digital technology practices with English as an Additional Language students in Australian schools
text_snippet: Teachers’ digital technology practices with English as an Additional Language students in Australian schools Abstract Digital technologies have shifted pedagogy, curriculum, and practice of English as an Additional Language (EAL) education notably in recent decades. Australia has a significant proportion of EAL students and a high rate of technology uptake in schools, but little is known about how teachers in Australia use digital technologies when working with their EAL students. This paper examines prevalent approaches to researching digital technology practices with EAL students in Australian schools, teachers’ pedagogical approaches to using digital technologies to support EAL education, and the affordances and constraints involved. Drawing on a systematic review of 16 publications, this study generates new insights into teachers’ everyday digital technology practices, which are often overlooked as most educational technology research focuses on interventionist studies. The review identifies a range of pedagogical practices, including digital multimodal composing, information seeking and analysis, and translation. However, these practices often highlight teachers’ use of multimodal technologies in supported contexts (via school-university research interventions) rather than in everyda

title: Primary school teachers’ epistemic cognition for moral education in the context of promoting social inclusion
text_snippet: Primary school teachers’ epistemic cognition for moral education in the context of promoting social inclusion Abstract While values education is one way primary schools can promote student social responsibility, little is understood about how teachers support children’s learning of moral values and how this changes throughout the years of primary school education. A growing body of research shows that teachers’ views about the nature of knowledge and knowing (epistemic cognition) mediate their approaches to teaching across a range of learning contexts. Using semi-structured interviews with Year 1 and Year 6 teachers, this paper explored the ways in which primary school teachers’ practices for moral education in one culturally diverse Australian school related to the ways in which they thought about knowledge and knowing. Findings showed that all teachers across both year levels described teaching strategies that went beyond imparting knowledge and that directed children’s behaviour in school towards supporting children to make meaning with respect to moral values and behaviours. Such strategies variously helped children to reflect, make decisions, engage with multiple perspectives, and express opinions/make judgments. title: Emotional and behavioural predictors of dropout intention and the moderating role of student appraisals among international students in Australian universities
text_snippet: Emotional and behavioural predictors of dropout intention and the moderating role of student appraisals among international students in Australian universities Abstract International student dropout presents a critical challenge for universities, with consequences for student well-being, institutional performance, and national economies. Despite their growing representation, limited research has investigated the psychological and institutional factors influencing dropout intention among international students. This study aimed to identify key psychological predictors of dropout intention and examine whether student appraisals of course content and institutional support moderate these relationships. To the authors’ knowledge, this is one of the first empirical investigations to explore these dynamics within an international student population in Australia. A total of 319 international students enrolled in Australian universities completed an online survey assessing mental health, resilience, mindfulness, filial piety, acculturation, financial stress, COVID-19 stress, sleep disturbance, and institutional perceptions. Hierarchical multiple regression and moderation analyses were conducted. title: Realities of imagined communities: collective autoethnography of identities and emotions of Japanese female international academics in Australian universities
text_snippet: Realities of imagined communities: collective autoethnography of identities and emotions of Japanese female international academics in Australian universities Abstract The present study is a collective autoethnography, exploring the academic identities of three international academics, all Japanese women who came to Australia in the late 1990s and have been working as Japanese language teachers and researchers in Australian universities for around 12 years. We began by writing about the experiences that had affected our academic identities, and the emotions triggered by those experiences, then exchanged these self-narratives, and discussed them as a group. We then wrote a second set of more reflective self-narratives. Here we collaboratively analyse these narratives and discussions using thematic analysis. After we started working full-time as academics, we faced the realities of Australian universities, our imagined communities. Lack of support from senior colleagues, the power of dominant White academics, the symbolic power of English, and the progress of neoliberalism have all triggered feelings of marginalisation in us. Our academic identities are complexly associated with sociopolitical aspects of universities, our immediate teaching and research contexts, and our linguistic and cultural backgrounds.

title: From the margins to the centre: how AI can transform education from the ground up
text_snippet: From the margins to the centre: how AI can transform education from the ground up Abstract For decades, Australia’s education system has failed Indigenous students. This paper contends that nearly 40 years of policy initiatives have targeted the wrong problem. The core issue is not the absence of Indigenous content or cultural awareness, but an inherited educational architecture structurally incapable of serving diverse learners. We propose leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) explicitly aligned with the cultural interface—the dynamic intersection between Indigenous and Western knowledge systems—to reconstruct education from the ground up. Indigenous Rangers are identified as a critical test case. Working daily across multiple cultural and language groups, in remote contexts, and at the intersection of knowledge traditions, Rangers hold advanced, practice-based expertise largely unrecognised by existing systems. Their work offers ideal conditions to test whether AI-enabled learning architectures can deliver rigorous, credentialed education in settings that conventional approaches have long failed to serve, providing a pathway for addressing the wider crisis in Indigenous education.

title: Reading assessment for autistic students: using a socio-ecological model to identify enablers and inhibitors for teachers in schools
text_snippet: Reading assessment for autistic students: using a socio-ecological model to identify enablers and inhibitors for teachers in schools Abstract Reading outcomes remain a priority for all students. While many general strategies have been offered to effectively assess reading in children in general, there is limited research exploring teachers’ assessment of reading for autistic students specifically. In this study, we were interested in how teachers assess reading for autistic students in their school contexts. We interviewed nine teachers, who worked across early childhood, primary and secondary schools, about what helps and what hinders reading assessment with autistic students. Using a socio-ecological model, we identified teachers' perceptions of individual, school, community, and macro-level factors related to reading assessment for autistic students. Teachers reported significant individual differences between autistic students, which resulted in them creating specific, individualised instructional and assessment resources. This put time and work pressure on the teachers despite their schools' support. Teachers also commented on needing more professional development in reading assessment for autistic students. title: Assessing the impact of COVID-19 and policy reforms on early childhood education in Victoria, Australia: a time series and spatial analysis
text_snippet: Assessing the impact of COVID-19 and policy reforms on early childhood education in Victoria, Australia: a time series and spatial analysis Abstract World-wide, COVID-19 significantly impacted the education sector, and specifically the Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) sector in Victoria, Australia. This caused declines in children’s enrolment due to restrictions that limited centre operations. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the Victorian government introduced the Best Start, Best Life reform (2024) to improve accessibility and equity in ECEC. The impact of the reform over three key periods is analysed: pre-COVID-19, COVID-19 and post-COVID-19, focusing on enrolment trends and affordability, through time series and regional spatial analysis. Findings indicate enrolments fell sharply during the COVID-19 closures, raising concerns about children’s developmental trajectories. The expected equitable distribution of enrolment benefits of the reform has not been uniformly achieved. Enrolment of children in rural areas has declined, while enrolment of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children has increased. Fee increases in areas close to metropolitan Melbourne have outpaced those in rural areas, where increases have been more gradual. title: Conducting research in initial teacher education programs: Reflections on a pilot intervention to enhance teacher readiness in an Australian university
text_snippet: Conducting research in initial teacher education programs: Reflections on a pilot intervention to enhance teacher readiness in an Australian university Abstract This study examines the process of embedding professional readiness initiatives within the context of an increasingly crowded initial teacher education (ITE) curriculum. Using a pilot intervention as a case, the study explores both the implementation of a program designed to foster readiness for professional practice and the challenges of conducting research within policy-driven and congested ITE programs. Readiness, conceptualised to be pre-service teachers’ perceived capacity to meet the professional, interpersonal, and pedagogical demands of classroom practice, was explored using a mixed-methods design framed by social exchange theory. The intervention comprised three components: completion of BRiTE resilience modules, participation in mixed-reality simulations, and engagement in online scenario-based learning activities. Data were collected through pre- and post-intervention surveys and open-ended feedback. Findings indicated modest increases in participants’ confidence and preparedness to teach, particularly in managing classrooms and communicating with parents. However, high attrition and limited engagement highlighted substantial institutional and structural barrier

title: Digital technologies and early childhood educator ‘control’
text_snippet: Digital technologies and early childhood educator ‘control’ Abstract In Australian early childhood education (ECE), recent policy requires children to be provided with opportunities to use digital technologies independently, safely, and in healthy ways. While there has been reluctance to integrate media and digital technologies, educators have taken up the challenge, with some experiencing difficulty in relinquishing control of digital devices. This article addresses the idea of control, using data from a case study involving 10 educators that was framed by a cultural studies of technologies approach. Educators discussed the benefits for children and educators of relinquishing control so children could use technologies independently and safely. Data were first analysed deductively for educator control and then inductively to identify six themes. Nine of the 10 participants were initially hesitant to use media and digital technologies in everyday practice. title: Children’s scientific literacy development in the early years: parental knowledge and understanding, confidence and practices at home
text_snippet: Children’s scientific literacy development in the early years: parental knowledge and understanding, confidence and practices at home Abstract Scientific literacy in early years can support children’s higher learning skills, such as logical thinking, problem-solving and conscious decision-making. Additionally, they can independently apply their scientific learning in a new context. The literature suggests that children’s scientific learning can be achieved with the support of adults, such as educators and parents. However, limited studies have examined how parents’ science knowledge and understanding, confidence, and science practices at home contribute to children’s scientific literacy development. This article explores parental science knowledge and understanding, confidence, and science play practices at home regarding children’s (4–5 years old) scientific literacy development. Customising the P-TABS instrument, this study collected self-reported responses from parents using a survey procedure at two preschool centres in New South Wales, Australia. title: Foundational research skills: perspectives from supervisors and students in a regional Australian university on graduate research education
text_snippet: Foundational research skills: perspectives from supervisors and students in a regional Australian university on graduate research education Abstract Many higher degree by research (HDR) students at our regional Australian university begin study after many years away from an academic environment. To support their transition, our university requires completion of mandatory coursework. We conducted an exploratory sequential mixed methods study to evaluate the coursework and identify the foundational research skills HDR students need. Phase 1 included semi-structured interviews with 11 experienced HDR supervisors on students’ capabilities, needs, and coursework experiences. Interviews were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings highlighted gaps in students’ institutional knowledge, personal and professional competencies, critical thinking and writing, and foundational research knowledge. Supervisors also noted structural challenges in term-based coursework that creates unintended tensions between HDR supervisors and students. Education was viewed as a shared responsibility. Phase 2 included surveys with HDR supervisors ( n = 40) and students ( n = 118) to further explore these themes.
